title: When your child answers in the other language: four things to say instead of pushing
description: A child who understands everything and answers in the other language has not stopped learning. Four responses that keep the conversation going instead of ending it.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: When your child answers in the other language: four things to say instead of pushing
body:
It happens around the age when school takes over: you speak in one language, your child answers in the other. Understanding is intact. Output has moved.

Pushing harder is the reflex, and it is the one thing that reliably backfires: the child learns that the minority language comes with a correction attached.

Four things to say instead.

Repeat, do not correct. Answer in the language you are building, using the sentence they could have said. Child says "I want water", you answer "¿quieres agua? Toma." Building English instead? Child says "quiero agua", you answer "you want water? Here." They hear the model without being told they were wrong. This one does most of the work.

Ask a question that cannot be answered with yes or no, in the language you are building: "¿Cuál quieres, el rojo o el azul?" — or "which one, the red or the blue?" A forced choice gets a word out, and the word comes back in the language you offered.

Give the word, then move on. If they stall looking for a word, say it and keep going. Holding the conversation hostage until the right word appears is what teaches children that speaking is expensive.

Name the moment, once, calmly, in your own words: at home we try in this language, and if it does not come out, we carry on anyway. One sentence a month. Not a rule recited at every meal.

Two more things that help, neither of them a conversation. Make the language useful: one activity the child likes that happens only in it — a call with a grandparent, a cartoon, a game. Usefulness beats encouragement. And keep practice short and physical: a child naming twelve objects they can touch is doing more than a child sitting through a worksheet.

What not to do: do not pretend you did not understand. Children read that instantly, and it turns the language into a negotiation.

Whichever direction your household runs in, the pattern is the same: model the sentence, offer a choice, hand over the word, and keep going.
